paragraphs: (Kept in shorthand.)

3 May. Bistritz. I left Munich at 8:35 p.m. on 1 May and reached Vienna early the next morning. We should have arrived at 6:46, but the train was an hour late. Budapest seems a wonderful place, judging by the glimpse I had of it from the train and the little I could see walking through its streets. I was afraid to go very far from the station, since we had arrived late and would leave as close to the scheduled time as possible. My impression was that we were leaving the West and entering the East. The westernmost of the splendid bridges over the Danube, which is here of noble width and depth, carried us into the traditions of Turkish rule.

We left in pretty good time and arrived after dark in Klausenburg. I stopped there for the night at the Hotel Royale. For dinner, or rather supper, I had a chicken prepared somehow with red pepper, which was very good but made me thirsty. (Note: get the recipe for Mina.) I asked the waiter, and he said it was called “paprika hendl,” and since it was a national dish, I should be able to get it anywhere in the Carpathians. I found my smattering of German very useful here. Indeed, I don’t know how I would get on without it.

Since I had some spare time in London, I visited the British Museum and searched through the books and maps in the library about Transylvania. It struck me that some advance knowledge of the country could hardly fail to be useful in dealing with a nobleman from there. I find that the district he named lies in the far east of the country, right on the border of three states, Transylvania, Moldavia, and Bukovina, in the middle of the Carpathian Mountains, one of the wildest and least known parts of Europe. I couldn’t find any map or book giving the exact location of Castle Dracula, since there are as yet no maps of this country to compare with our own Ordnance Survey maps. But I found that Bistritz, the post town named by Count Dracula, is a fairly well-known place. I’ll record some of my notes here, since they may refresh my memory when I talk over my travels with Mina.

The population of Transylvania includes four distinct nationalities: Saxons in the south, and mixed with them the Wallachs, who are descended from the Dacians; Magyars in the west; and Szekelys in the east and north. I am going among the last of these, who claim to be descended from Attila and the Huns. This may be so, since when the Magyars conquered the country in the eleventh century, they found the Huns already settled there. I read that every known superstition in the world is gathered into the horseshoe of the Carpathians, as if it were the center of some kind of whirlpool of the imagination. If so, my stay may be very interesting. (Note: I must ask the Count all about them.)

I didn’t sleep well, though my bed was comfortable enough, because I had all sorts of strange dreams. A dog howled under my window all night, which may have had something to do with it, or it may have been the paprika, because I had to drink all the water in my carafe and was still thirsty. Toward morning I fell asleep and was woken by continuous knocking at my door, so I suppose I must have been sleeping soundly then. For breakfast I had more paprika and a kind of porridge of corn flour that they said was “mamaliga,” and eggplant stuffed with minced meat, a very excellent dish they call “impletata.” (Note: get the recipe for this too.) I had to hurry through breakfast, because the train left a little before eight, or rather it should have, since after rushing to the station at 7:30, I had to sit in the carriage for more than an hour before we started moving. It seems to me that the farther east you go, the less punctual the trains are. What must they be like in China?

All day long we seemed to dawdle through a country full of beauty of every kind. Sometimes we saw little towns or castles on top of steep hills, like the ones in old illuminated manuscripts. Sometimes we ran alongside rivers and streams that seemed, from the wide stony margins on each side, to be subject to great floods. It takes a lot of water, running strong, to sweep the edge of a river clean. At every station there were groups of people, sometimes crowds, dressed in all sorts of clothing. Some looked just like the peasants at home or those I saw in France and Germany, with short jackets, round hats, and homemade trousers, but others were very picturesque. The women looked pretty, except when you got close to them, but they were very clumsy around the waist. They all had full white sleeves of some kind, and most of them wore big belts with a lot of strips of something fluttering from them, like the dresses in a ballet, though of course there were petticoats underneath. The strangest figures we saw were the Slovaks, who were wilder than the rest, with their big cowboy hats, great baggy dirty-white trousers, white linen shirts, and enormous heavy leather belts, nearly a foot wide, all studded with brass nails. They wore high boots with their trousers tucked into them, and had long black hair and heavy black mustaches. They are very picturesque but not very prepossessing. On stage they would be taken at once for some old Oriental band of bandits. They are, however, I’m told, very harmless and rather lacking in natural self-assertion.

It was just after dusk when we got to Bistritz, a very interesting old town. Being practically on the frontier (the Borgo Pass leads from it into Bukovina), it has had a very stormy history, and it certainly shows the marks of it. Fifty years ago a series of great fires struck five separate times, causing terrible destruction. At the very beginning of the seventeenth century it endured a three-week siege and lost 13,000 people, the casualties of the war itself being added to by famine and disease.

Count Dracula had told me to go to the Golden Krone Hotel, which I found, to my great delight, to be thoroughly old-fashioned, since of course I wanted to see as much as I could of the ways of the country. I was clearly expected, because when I got near the door, I came face to face with a cheerful-looking elderly woman in the usual peasant dress: a white undergarment with a long double apron, front and back, of colored cloth, fitting almost too tightly to be modest. When I came close, she bowed and said, “The English gentleman?” “Yes,” I said, “Jonathan Harker.” She smiled and gave some message to an elderly man in white shirtsleeves, who had followed her to the door. He went off but returned immediately with a letter:

“My friend. Welcome to the Carpathians. I am anxiously expecting you. Sleep well tonight. At three tomorrow the coach will leave for Bukovina, and a place on it has been kept for you. At the Borgo Pass my carriage will be waiting for you and will bring you to me. I trust your journey from London has been a happy one, and that you will enjoy your stay in my beautiful land.
“Your friend,
“DRACULA.”

4 May. I found that my landlord had received a letter from the Count telling him to secure the best seat on the coach for me, but when I asked about the details, he seemed rather reluctant and pretended he couldn’t understand my German. This couldn’t be true, because until then he had understood it perfectly. At least, he had answered my questions exactly as if he had. He and his wife, the old lady who had welcomed me, looked at each other in a frightened sort of way. He mumbled that the money had been sent in a letter and that was all he knew. When I asked if he knew Count Dracula and could tell me anything about his castle, both he and his wife crossed themselves, and, saying they knew nothing at all, simply refused to speak any further. It was so close to departure time that I had no chance to ask anyone else, because it was all very mysterious and not at all comforting.
Just before I left, the old lady came up to my room and said in a very hysterical way:

“Must you go? Oh, young sir, must you go?” She was in such an agitated state that she seemed to have lost her grip on what German she knew and mixed it up with some other language I didn’t know at all. I could just follow her by asking many questions. When I told her that I had to go at once and that I was on important business, she asked again:
“Do you know what day it is?” I answered that it was the fourth of May. She shook her head and said again:
“Oh, yes! I know that! I know that, but do you know what day it is?” When I said I didn’t understand, she went on:

“It is the eve of St. George’s Day. Don’t you know that tonight, when the clock strikes midnight, all the evil things in the world will have free rein? Do you know where you are going, and what you are going to?” She was in such obvious distress that I tried to comfort her, but without effect. Finally she went down on her knees and begged me not to go, or at least to wait a day or two before setting out. It was all very ridiculous, but I didn’t feel comfortable. However, there was business to be done, and I could let nothing interfere with it. So I tried to raise her up and said, as gravely as I could, that I thanked her, but my duty was pressing and I had to go. She then got up and dried her eyes, and taking a crucifix from her neck, offered it to me. I didn’t know what to do, since, as an English churchman, I have been taught to regard such things as somewhat idolatrous, and yet it seemed so ungracious to refuse an old lady who meant so well and was in such a state of mind. She must have seen the doubt in my face, because she put the rosary around my neck and said, “For your mother’s sake,” and left the room. I am writing up this part of the diary while I wait for the coach, which is, of course, late, and the crucifix is still around my neck. Whether it is the old lady’s fear, or the many ghostly traditions of this place, or the crucifix itself, I don’t know, but I don’t feel nearly as easy in my mind as usual. If this book should reach Mina before I do, let it carry my goodbye. Here comes the coach!

5 May. The Castle. The gray of morning has passed, and the sun is high over the distant horizon, which looks jagged, whether with trees or hills I can’t tell, because it is so far off that big things and little ones are mixed together. I’m not sleepy, and since I’m not to be called until I wake, I naturally write until sleep comes. There are many odd things to put down, and lest whoever reads them imagines I dined too well before leaving Bistritz, let me record my dinner exactly. I dined on what they called “robber steak”: bits of bacon, onion, and beef, seasoned with red pepper, strung on sticks and roasted over the fire, in the simple style of the London cat’s-meat man! The wine was Golden Mediasch, which leaves a strange sting on the tongue that is not unpleasant. I had only a couple of glasses of this and nothing else.

When I got on the coach, the driver hadn’t taken his seat yet, and I saw him talking with the landlady. They were obviously talking about me, because every now and then they looked at me, and some of the people sitting on the bench outside the door (which they call by a name meaning “word-bearer”) came over and listened, then looked at me, most of them with pity. I could hear many words repeated often, strange words, since there were many nationalities in the crowd. So I quietly took my multilingual dictionary out of my bag and looked them up. I must say they weren’t cheering, because among them were “Ordog,” meaning Satan, “pokol,” meaning hell, “stregoica,” meaning witch, and “vrolok” and “vlkoslak,” both of which mean the same thing, one being Slovak and the other Serbian for something that is either a werewolf or a vampire. (Note: I must ask the Count about these superstitions.)

When we set off, the crowd around the inn door, which had by now grown quite large, all made the sign of the cross and pointed two fingers at me. With some difficulty I got a fellow passenger to tell me what they meant. At first he wouldn’t answer, but when he learned I was English, he explained that it was a charm or protection against the evil eye. This wasn’t very pleasant for me, just setting out for an unknown place to meet an unknown man, but everyone seemed so kind-hearted and so sorrowful and sympathetic that I couldn’t help being touched. I’ll never forget my last glimpse of the inn yard and its crowd of picturesque figures, all crossing themselves, standing around the wide archway, with its background of rich foliage of oleander and orange trees in green tubs clustered in the middle of the yard. Then our driver, whose wide linen trousers covered the whole front of the driver’s seat (“gotza” they call them), cracked his big whip over his four small horses, which ran side by side, and we set off on our journey.

I soon lost sight and memory of ghostly fears in the beauty of the scene as we drove along, though if I had understood the language, or rather languages, my fellow passengers were speaking, I might not have shaken them off so easily. Before us lay a green sloping land full of forests and woods, with here and there steep hills crowned with clumps of trees or with farmhouses, their blank gable ends to the road. There was everywhere a bewildering mass of fruit blossom: apple, plum, pear, cherry. As we drove by, I could see the green grass under the trees spangled with fallen petals. In and out among these green hills of what they call here the “Mittel Land” ran the road, disappearing as it swept round a grassy curve or was shut out by the straggling ends of pine woods that ran down the hillsides here and there like tongues of flame. The road was rough, but we seemed to fly over it with feverish haste. I couldn’t understand then what the haste meant, but the driver was clearly determined to lose no time in reaching Borgo Prund. I was told that this road is excellent in summer, but that it hadn’t yet been put in order after the winter snows. In this respect it differs from most roads in the Carpathians, because there is an old tradition that they are not to be kept in too good repair. In the old days the Hospadars wouldn’t repair them, lest the Turks should think they were preparing to bring in foreign troops and so hasten the war that was always really on the verge of breaking out.

Beyond the green swelling hills of the Mittel Land rose mighty slopes of forest up to the lofty heights of the Carpathians themselves. Right and left they towered over us, with the afternoon sun falling full upon them and bringing out all the glorious colors of this beautiful range: deep blue and purple in the shadows of the peaks, green and brown where grass and rock mingled, and an endless view of jagged rock and pointed crags, until these were themselves lost in the distance, where the snowy peaks rose grandly. Here and there seemed to be mighty rifts in the mountains, through which, as the sun began to sink, we saw now and again the white gleam of falling water. One of my companions touched my arm as we swept around the base of a hill and opened up the lofty, snow-covered peak of a mountain, which seemed, as we wound along our serpentine way, to be right in front of us:
“Look! Isten szek!” (“God’s seat!”) And he crossed himself reverently.

As we wound on our endless way, with the sun sinking lower and lower behind us, the shadows of evening began to creep around us. This was emphasized by the fact that the snowy mountaintop still held the sunset and seemed to glow with a delicate, cool pink. Here and there we passed Czechs and Slovaks, all in picturesque dress, but I noticed that goiter was painfully common. By the roadside there were many crosses, and as we swept by, my companions all crossed themselves. Here and there a peasant man or woman knelt before a shrine and didn’t even turn around as we approached, but seemed, in the self-surrender of devotion, to have neither eyes nor ears for the outside world. There were many things new to me: for instance, haystacks in the trees, and here and there very beautiful masses of weeping birch, their white trunks shining like silver through the delicate green of the leaves. Now and again we passed a ladder wagon, the ordinary peasant’s cart, with its long, snakelike spine, designed to suit the unevenness of the road. On this were sure to be seated quite a group of peasants going home, the Czechs in their white sheepskins and the Slovaks in their colored ones, the latter carrying their long staffs like lances, with an axe at the end. As evening fell it began to get very cold, and the growing twilight seemed to merge the gloom of the trees, oak, beech, and pine, into one dark mistiness, though in the valleys that ran deep between the spurs of the hills, as we climbed through the Pass, the dark firs stood out here and there against the background of late-lying snow. Sometimes, as the road was cut through pine woods that seemed in the darkness to be closing in on us, great masses of grayness, scattered here and there over the trees, produced a peculiarly weird and solemn effect, which carried on the thoughts and grim fancies stirred up earlier in the evening, when the falling sunset threw into strange relief the ghostlike clouds that seem to wind ceaselessly through the valleys of the Carpathians. Sometimes the hills were so steep that, despite our driver’s haste, the horses could only go slowly. I wanted to get down and walk up them, as we do at home, but the driver wouldn’t hear of it. “No, no,” he said. “You must not walk here. The dogs are too fierce.” And then he added, with what he clearly meant as grim humor (because he looked around to catch the approving smile of the others), “And you may have enough of such things before you go to sleep.” The only stop he would make was a moment’s pause to light his lamps.

When it grew dark, there seemed to be some excitement among the passengers, and they kept speaking to him, one after another, as though urging him to go faster. He lashed the horses mercilessly with his long whip and, with wild cries of encouragement, urged them on to greater effort. Then through the darkness I could see a patch of gray light ahead of us, as though there were a gap in the hills. The passengers’ excitement grew. The crazy coach rocked on its great leather springs and swayed like a boat tossed on a stormy sea. I had to hold on. The road grew more level, and we seemed to fly along. Then the mountains seemed to come closer on each side and frown down on us. We were entering the Borgo Pass. One by one several of the passengers offered me gifts, which they pressed on me with an earnestness that wouldn’t take no for an answer. They were certainly odd and varied gifts, but each was given in simple good faith, with a kind word and a blessing and that strange mixture of fearful gestures I had seen outside the hotel at Bistritz: the sign of the cross and the protection against the evil eye. Then, as we flew along, the driver leaned forward, and on each side the passengers, craning over the edge of the coach, peered eagerly into the darkness. It was obvious that something very exciting was either happening or expected, but though I asked each passenger, no one would give me the slightest explanation. This state of excitement continued for some little time, and at last we saw the Pass opening out before us on the eastern side. There were dark, rolling clouds overhead, and in the air the heavy, oppressive feeling of thunder. It seemed as though the mountain range had separated two atmospheres and we had now entered the thundery one. I was by now looking out myself for the vehicle that was to take me to the Count. Each moment I expected to see the glare of lamps through the blackness, but all was dark. The only light was the flickering rays of our own lamps, in which the steam from our hard-driven horses rose in a white cloud. We could see the sandy road lying white before us, but there was no sign of a vehicle on it. The passengers drew back with a sigh of gladness that seemed to mock my own disappointment. I was already thinking about what I had best do when the driver, looking at his watch, said something to the others that I could hardly hear, it was spoken so quietly and in so low a tone. I thought it was “An hour less than the time.” Then, turning to me, he said in German worse than my own:

“There is no carriage here. The gentleman is not expected after all. He will now go on to Bukovina and return tomorrow or the next day, better the next day.” While he was speaking, the horses began to neigh and snort and plunge wildly, so that the driver had to hold them back. Then, amid a chorus of screams from the peasants and a universal crossing of themselves, a carriage with four horses drove up behind us, overtook us, and pulled up beside the coach. I could see by the flash of our lamps, as the rays fell on them, that the horses were coal-black and splendid animals. They were driven by a tall man with a long brown beard and a great black hat, which seemed to hide his face from us. I could only see the gleam of a pair of very bright eyes, which seemed red in the lamplight, as he turned to us. He said to the driver:
“You are early tonight, my friend.” The man stammered in reply:
“The English gentleman was in a hurry,” to which the stranger replied:

“That is why, I suppose, you wanted him to go on to Bukovina. You cannot deceive me, my friend. I know too much, and my horses are swift.” As he spoke he smiled, and the lamplight fell on a hard-looking mouth with very red lips and sharp teeth as white as ivory. One of my companions whispered to another the line from Bürger’s “Lenore”:
“Denn die Todten reiten schnell” (“For the dead travel fast.”)

The strange driver clearly heard the words, because he looked up with a gleaming smile. The passenger turned his face away, at the same time putting out two fingers and crossing himself. “Give me the gentleman’s luggage,” said the driver, and with extreme eagerness my bags were handed out and put in the carriage. Then I climbed down from the side of the coach, since the carriage was close alongside, the driver helping me with a hand that caught my arm in a grip of steel. His strength must have been prodigious. Without a word he shook his reins, the horses turned, and we swept into the darkness of the Pass. As I looked back, I saw by the light of the lamps the steam from the coach’s horses, and projected against it the figures of my late companions crossing themselves. Then the driver cracked his whip and called to his horses, and off they swept on their way to Bukovina. As they sank into the darkness, I felt a strange chill and a lonely feeling came over me, but a cloak was thrown over my shoulders and a rug across my knees, and the driver said in excellent German:

“The night is chill, sir, and my master the Count told me to take every care of you. There is a flask of slivovitz (the plum brandy of the country) under the seat, if you should want it.” I didn’t take any, but it was a comfort to know it was there all the same. I felt a little strange and more than a little frightened. I think if there had been any alternative, I would have taken it instead of continuing that unknown night journey. The carriage went at a hard pace straight ahead, then we made a complete turn and went along another straight road. It seemed to me that we were simply going over the same ground again and again, so I took note of a prominent landmark and found that this was so. I would have liked to ask the driver what all this meant, but I really was afraid to, because I thought that, placed as I was, any protest would have no effect if there was an intention to delay. By and by, however, since I was curious to know how time was passing, I struck a match and by its flame looked at my watch. It was within a few minutes of midnight. This gave me a kind of shock, because I suppose the general superstition about midnight was increased by my recent experiences. I waited with a sick feeling of suspense.

Then a dog began to howl somewhere in a farmhouse far down the road, a long, agonized wailing, as if from fear. The sound was taken up by another dog, and then another and another, until, carried on the wind that now sighed softly through the Pass, a wild howling began that seemed to come from all over the country, as far as the imagination could grasp it through the gloom of the night. At the first howl the horses began to strain and rear, but the driver spoke soothingly to them and they quieted down, though they shivered and sweated as though after a runaway from sudden fright. Then, far off in the distance, from the mountains on each side of us, began a louder and sharper howling, that of wolves, which affected both the horses and me in the same way. I felt like jumping out of the carriage and running, while they reared again and plunged madly, so that the driver had to use all his great strength to keep them from bolting. In a few minutes, however, my own ears got used to the sound, and the horses grew quiet enough that the driver was able to get down and stand before them. He petted and soothed them and whispered something in their ears, as I have heard of horse-tamers doing, with extraordinary effect, because under his caresses they became quite manageable again, though they still trembled. The driver again took his seat and, shaking his reins, started off at a great pace. This time, after going to the far side of the Pass, he suddenly turned down a narrow road that ran sharply to the right.

Soon we were hemmed in by trees, which in places arched right over the road until we passed as through a tunnel, and again great frowning rocks guarded us boldly on either side. Though we were sheltered, we could hear the rising wind, because it moaned and whistled through the rocks and the branches of the trees crashed together as we swept along. It grew colder and colder still, and fine, powdery snow began to fall, so that soon we and everything around us were covered with a white blanket. The keen wind still carried the howling of the dogs, though it grew fainter as we went on our way. The baying of the wolves sounded nearer and nearer, as though they were closing in on us from every side. I grew dreadfully afraid, and the horses shared my fear. The driver, however, wasn’t in the least disturbed. He kept turning his head to left and right, but I couldn’t see anything through the darkness.

Suddenly, away on our left, I saw a faint flickering blue flame. The driver saw it at the same moment. He stopped the horses at once and, jumping to the ground, disappeared into the darkness. I didn’t know what to do, especially since the howling of the wolves was growing closer. But while I wondered, the driver suddenly reappeared and, without a word, took his seat, and we resumed our journey. I think I must have fallen asleep and kept dreaming of the incident, because it seemed to repeat endlessly, and now, looking back, it is like a kind of awful nightmare. Once the flame appeared so near the road that even in the darkness around us I could watch the driver’s movements. He went quickly to where the blue flame rose (it must have been very faint, because it didn’t seem to light up the place around it at all) and, gathering a few stones, arranged them into some kind of pattern. Once there was a strange optical effect: when he stood between me and the flame, he didn’t block it, because I could see its ghostly flicker all the same. This startled me, but since the effect was only momentary, I took it that my eyes were deceiving me as I strained through the darkness. Then for a time there were no blue flames, and we sped onward through the gloom with the howling of the wolves around us, as though they were following in a moving circle.

At last there came a time when the driver went farther afield than he had yet gone, and during his absence the horses began to tremble worse than ever and to snort and scream with fright. I couldn’t see any cause for it, because the howling of the wolves had stopped altogether. But just then the moon, sailing through the black clouds, appeared behind the jagged crest of a beetling, pine-covered rock, and by its light I saw around us a ring of wolves, with white teeth and lolling red tongues, with long, sinewy limbs and shaggy hair. They were a hundred times more terrible in the grim silence that held them than even when they howled. As for me, I felt a sort of paralysis of fear. It is only when a man finds himself face to face with such horrors that he can understand their true meaning.

All at once the wolves began to howl as though the moonlight had had some peculiar effect on them. The horses jumped about and reared and looked helplessly around with eyes that rolled in a way painful to see, but the living ring of terror encircled them on every side, and they had no choice but to stay within it. I called to the coachman to come, because it seemed to me that our only chance was to try to break out through the ring, and to help his approach. I shouted and beat the side of the carriage, hoping that the noise would scare the wolves from that side and give him a chance of reaching the carriage. How he got there, I don’t know, but I heard his voice raised in a tone of imperious command, and looking toward the sound, I saw him standing in the road. As he swept his long arms, as though brushing aside some invisible obstacle, the wolves fell back and back farther still. Just then a heavy cloud passed across the face of the moon, so that we were again in darkness.

When I could see again, the driver was climbing into the carriage and the wolves had disappeared. This was all so strange and uncanny that a dreadful fear came over me, and I was afraid to speak or move. The time seemed endless as we swept on our way, now in almost complete darkness, because the rolling clouds hid the moon. We kept climbing, with occasional stretches of quick descent, but mostly always climbing. Suddenly I realized that the driver was in the act of pulling up the horses in the courtyard of a vast ruined castle, from whose tall black windows came no ray of light, and whose broken battlements showed a jagged line against the moonlit sky.
